quotes.text: Keeping everything creates a different problem. Old content piles up, people struggle to find the current version.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: Challenges the common instinct that keeping everything forever is the safe option.

quotes.text: So retention isn't only about keeping content, it's also about removing content when there's no reason to keep it.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: Summarises the dual purpose of retention in one clear sentence.

quotes.text: Start with the reason. Why does this content exist? Who needs it? Is there a legal, regulatory, financial or business reason to keep it?
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: Gives a practical, reason-first method for defining retention rules.

quotes.text: Use static scope when the target is simple and stable. Use adaptive scope when the target should move as people, groups or sites change.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: Offers a crisp rule of thumb for choosing between static and adaptive scopes.

quotes.text: Retention decides how long content must remain. It doesn't decide who can open the document. It doesn't decide whether someone can share it with an outside person.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: Clearly separates lifecycle management from access and sharing controls.

chapters.title: The data lifecycle from creation to disposal

takeaways: Define retention by business, legal or regulatory reason first and only then pick the number of years.
Use retention policies for broad location-wide rules, retention labels for individual items with special lifespans, and adaptive scopes when the audience changes over time.
When rules overlap, retention beats deletion, the longest retention period wins and the shortest deletion period applies once no retention remains.
hook: Keeping every email, chat and file forever feels safe, but it piles up risk, clutter and discovery effort. This episode explains Microsoft Purview Data Lifecycle Management for Microsoft 365 admins and compliance teams in plain English. You will learn how retention policies, retention labels, scopes and conflict rules fit together into one rule book.
